15.title: why there's fire in every church
15.hook: why there's fire in every church
15.howItsDone: Catholics light votive candles in churches for people they are praying for, keep a sanctuary lamp burning near the tabernacle, and light the paschal candle at the Easter Vigil, baptisms and funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sunday, the gift inside the obligation. Your line was one day that isn't yours to fill. Week three starts with fire. Day fifteen.
screen: `ONE DAY THAT ISN'T YOURS TO FILL.` → `WEEK THREE.`

segments.voice: Every building has lights now. Switches, LEDs, the glow of exit signs. And yet step into a Catholic church at noon, in a city with perfect electricity, and there's still fire. Two candles on the altar. A tall one near the front. Rows of little flames in a side corner, flickering, somebody's coins in the box beside them. And one small red lamp that never seems to go out. It isn't for seeing. Nobody needs a candle to read anymore. So why is there fire in every church?
screen: `PERFECT ELECTRICITY.` → `AND STILL, FIRE.` → `IT ISN'T FOR SEEING.`

segments.voice: Start with what Jesus says in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness." So a candle in a church is a small sermon without words. Light in the dark. And every candle there has its own job. The candles on or near the altar are lit for Mass. The tall one is the Easter candle, the paschal candle. On the night before Easter, Catholics gather outside in the dark, light a new fire, and carry this one candle into a black church while someone sings, three times, light of Christ. Then the flame is passed from candle to candle through the whole crowd until the room is full of light. The same candle stands near the font at baptisms, and beside the coffin at funerals. The little red lamp is the one from day two: the sanctuary lamp, burning near the tabernacle as a sign that Christ is present there. And the rows in the corner? Votive candles, from the Latin votum, a vow or a prayer. Someone lights one for a sick mother, a job interview, a child who's struggling, a friend who died. The flame keeps burning after they walk out the door. Some people put it this way: the candle keeps praying after I leave. In Catholic teaching, the wax does nothing by itself. It's a way of saying: this person matters, and I'm not done hoping.
screen: `I AM THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.` · `THE EASTER CANDLE.` · `THE RED LAMP: HE IS HERE.` · `VOTIVE — A VOW, A PRAYER.` · then, large: `THIS PERSON MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If there's a candle nearby, you can light it. If not, just picture one. Think of one person who could use some light right now. See their face above the flame. You don't have to fix anything. Just hold them there while it burns, breathing slowly. If you pray, you can pray for them.
Candles. Light in the dark: the Easter candle, the sanctuary lamp, and the votive flame that keeps praying after you leave. Fifteenth word.
Your line: light a candle for someone. The flame keeps hoping after you've gone. Day fifteen.

16.title: the women went first
16.tomorrow: the rich kid who gave his clothes back
16.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Easter with the Easter Vigil on Saturday night and Mass on Easter Sunday, and keep the Easter season for fifty days, until Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday: candles, and the Easter flame carried into a dark church. Your line was light a candle for someone. Today, the morning that flame is for. Day sixteen.

Very early on a Sunday morning, near Jerusalem. Jesus has been executed and buried. The men who followed him are nowhere in this scene. A few women are walking to a tomb cut in the rock, carrying spices to anoint a body. That's what you did for someone you loved. On the way, they realize they have a problem. A great stone has been rolled across the entrance. In Mark's Gospel, they ask each other: "Who shall roll us back the stone from the door of the sepulchre?" They go anyway. They don't have a plan. They just go.
screen: `VERY EARLY. A SUNDAY.` → `A FEW WOMEN, WITH SPICES.` → `WHO WILL ROLL BACK THE STONE?`

segments.voice: When they get there, the stone is already rolled away. The tomb is empty. In one telling, two men in shining clothes ask them why they're looking for the living among the dead, and say, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "He is not here, but is risen." Every Gospel tells it a little differently: how many women, how many angels, who sees what first. But all four agree on one thing: women were the first witnesses at the empty tomb. Some scholars point out that a woman's word counted for less in that world, which makes the detail stand out. And the men, one Gospel says, didn't believe them at first: the women's words seemed like idle tales. In another telling, Mary Magdalene stays behind at the tomb, crying, and meets the risen Jesus himself, and doesn't recognize him until he says her name. Then he sends her to tell the others. That's why Catholic tradition calls her the apostle to the apostles: the one sent to the ones who would be sent. Catholics believe the resurrection is the center of everything: that Jesus truly rose from the dead, and that death is not the end of the story. It's why, as day fourteen said, Christians gather on Sunday: every Sunday keeps a little of Easter. Easter itself isn't just one day. It's a season of fifty days, longer than Lent. In Spanish, Italian and French, the feast's name comes from Pascha, the Passover: Pascua, Pasqua, Pâques. And look at the order of that morning. The women worried about the stone the whole way there. By the time they arrived, it had already been moved.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of one stone you're worried about: something ahead that feels too heavy to move. A conversation, a bill, a diagnosis, a decision. Picture yourself walking toward it anyway, like the women did, without a plan. Breathe slowly as you walk. You don't have to solve it. Just keep walking. If you pray, you can bring it to God.
Easter. The feast of the resurrection, the empty tomb, and the women who were sent to tell. Sixteenth word.
Your line: the stone is already moved. The women only found out because they went anyway. Day sixteen.

17.title: the rich kid who gave his clothes back
17.hook: the rich kid who gave his clothes back
17.tomorrow: the word Pope Francis kept saying
17.howItsDone: Catholics keep a feast day for Saint Francis each year, and some parishes bless pets and animals around it; the Peace Prayer, first printed in 1912, is often prayed in his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Easter, the women, and the stone already moved. Today, one of the saints from day five, up close. Day seventeen.

Italy, the Middle Ages. A town on a hill called Assisi. There's a young man there everyone knows: the son of a rich cloth merchant, good clothes, good parties, the one who pays for everybody's dinner. He dreams of being a knight. He goes off to a war with the next town, gets captured, spends a long stretch in a prison cell, and comes home sick. And something in him has changed. He starts giving things away. Money, cloth from his father's shop. His father is furious, and drags him in front of the bishop of Assisi, in the town square, to get his property back. What the son does next is why people still know his name.
screen: `ASSISI, A TOWN ON A HILL.` → `THE RICH MERCHANT'S SON.` → `DRAGGED BEFORE THE BISHOP.`

segments.voice: His name was Francesco. We say Francis. According to the stories written down by his early followers, he stood in front of the bishop and the whole town, took off his clothes, every piece, and handed them back to his father. And he said, in effect: until now I called you my father. From now on I'll say our Father, who art in heaven. The bishop covered him with his own cloak. Francis walked out of town with nothing. What came next is the part people forget. He didn't become a hermit. He went toward the people everyone avoided. The stories say that once, riding outside town, he met a man with leprosy, a disease that made people outcasts, and instead of riding past, he got down and kissed his hand. Later he wrote that what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness. He gathered friends who lived poor, preached in the streets and cared for the sick. They became the Franciscans, who still carry his name. Near the end of his life he wrote a song, the Canticle of the Creatures, praising God for brother sun and sister moon, even sister death. Now today's line: lord, make me an instrument. It opens the prayer that bears his name, make me an instrument of your peace. Here's the honest part. As far as anyone can tell, Francis didn't write it. Its first known printing is in a small French magazine in 1912, with no author's name. His name was attached to it later. Francis's own words are in the Canticle.
screen: `HE GAVE THE CLOTHES BACK.` · `TOWARD THE PEOPLE EVERYONE AVOIDED.` · `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.` · `THE PRAYER HE PROBABLY DIDN'T WRITE.` · then, large: `MAKE ME AN INSTRUMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Get comfortable and let your breath slow down. Think of one thing you're holding on to a little too tightly. It doesn't have to be big. A grudge counts. With each breath out, imagine loosening your grip on it, the way Francis handed his clothes back. If you pray, you can say the line: lord, make me an instrument.
Francis. Francis of Assisi, the rich kid who gave it all back and went toward the outcasts. Seventeenth word.
Your line: lord, make me an instrument. The prayer borrowed his name; the life was his own. See you tomorrow.

18.title: the word Pope Francis kept saying
18.hook: the word Pope Francis kept saying
18.howItsDone: Catholics practice the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, visiting the sick and forgiving injuries, and celebrate Divine Mercy Sunday on the Sunday after Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Francis of Assisi, the rich kid who gave it all back. Your line was lord, make me an instrument. Today, the pope who took his name. Day eighteen.

In 2013, a man from Buenos Aires who used to ride the bus to work became pope and took a name no pope had ever used: Francis, after the saint from Assisi you met yesterday. One word kept coming up, in sermons, in interviews, off the cuff to crowds. He called a whole year after it. He titled a book after it. Asked once, early on, to describe himself, he said, in effect: a sinner the Lord has looked upon. Pope Francis led the Church until his death in 2025. Today, his word: mercy.
screen: `A POPE WHO RODE THE BUS.` → `ONE WORD KEPT COMING UP.` → `A SINNER THE LORD LOOKED UPON.`

segments.voice: The Latin word is misericordia. Inside it are two smaller words: miser, wretched, in trouble, and cor, the heart. Mercy is a heart that goes out to someone in misery. Not a verdict. A heart. The Bible's Hebrew has a word for it that comes from the word for a mother's womb, the kind of love you feel for a child you carried. Luke's Gospel puts it at the center of what Jesus asks, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." Pope Francis took his motto from an old sermon by Bede, an English monk, about the day Jesus called Matthew, a tax collector everyone despised. Jesus looked at him, Bede says, with mercy, and chose him. In Latin: miserando atque eligendo. By having mercy, and by choosing. Francis said that was his own story. That's where today's line comes from. Francis kept saying that people who can't show mercy have often never let themselves receive it. You can't give away what you've never been handed. So the first step is to accept it: to let God, or someone, look at you with mercy and choose you anyway, the way Jesus looked at Matthew. For some people, the hardest one to show mercy to is themselves. Then it flows outward: forgiving, feeding, visiting, going toward people in trouble. Catholics call these the works of mercy. Francis of Assisi kissing the leper's hand was the same heart. And confession, from day three, is the Church saying it out loud: you're forgiven.
screen: `MISERICORDIA — A HEART FOR THE WRETCHED.` · `BE YE THEREFORE MERCIFUL.` · `BY HAVING MERCY, AND BY CHOOSING.` · `YOU CAN'T GIVE WHAT YOU WERE NEVER HANDED.` · then, large: `START WITH YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Bring to mind one thing you haven't quite forgiven yourself for, if there is one. Something small is fine. Picture someone who loves you looking at it, and at you, without flinching. Not excusing it. Just looking at you with a heart that goes out to you. Breathe slowly, and let yourself be looked at like that. If you pray, you can let that look be God's.
Mercy. Misericordia: a heart that goes out to someone in trouble, received first, then given away. Eighteenth word.
Your line: start with yourself. Mercy received is the only kind you can pass on. Day eighteen.

19.title: one, holy, catholic
19.hook: one, holy, catholic — the small-c word means universal
19.tomorrow: the saint who wrote about prayer like a friendship
19.howItsDone: Every Sunday at Mass, Catholics profess a creed, usually the Nicene Creed, including belief in "one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church," and pray for the pope and the local bishop by name.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mercy, a heart that goes out to someone in trouble. Your line was start with yourself. Today, the small word in the Church's own name. Day nineteen.

A Catholic Mass in Lagos. In Manila. In a tiny village in Poland. In a strip-mall parish in Texas. The language is different. The music is wildly different: drums, organs, guitars, choirs in five-part harmony. But a regular would know where they were almost at once. The readings, the peace, the table. The same shape, in a language you don't speak. Every Sunday, Catholics say a creed that calls the Church one, holy, catholic and apostolic. Today, the small-c word in that line, and what it actually means.
screen: `LAGOS, MANILA, POLAND, TEXAS.` → `THE SAME SHAPE.` → `ONE, HOLY, CATHOLIC.`

segments.voice: Start with church. In the New Testament the Greek word is ekklesia, from a verb meaning to call out. It meant an assembly, people called out of their houses to gather. So the Church, first of all, isn't a building. It's the people who were called. Now the small-c word. Catholic comes from the Greek katholikos, from kath' holou: according to the whole. Universal. Early in Christian history, a bishop named Ignatius of Antioch was being taken to Rome under guard, to be executed. On the way he wrote letters to the churches. In one of them he writes that wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic Church. He meant the whole Church, everywhere, gathered around Christ. The creed said at Sunday Mass puts four words side by side. One: many countries, one faith. Holy: set apart for God, even though, as day five said, its people are far from perfect. Catholic: for everyone, everywhere. Apostolic: going back to the apostles. Catholics believe their Church is one family under the pope, the bishop of Rome, successor of Peter. And that family is more varied than it looks. Alongside the Latin Church there are Eastern Catholic Churches, with their own liturgies and traditions, united with Rome. Other Christians say these creed words too. Orthodox Christians say catholic and mean the Orthodox Church. In Protestant churches that say the creed, it usually means the whole Church of Christ across every denomination. For Catholics, Ignatius's line still sets the size of the word: wherever Christ is.
screen: `EKKLESIA — THE ONES CALLED OUT.` · `KATHOLIKOS — ACCORDING TO THE WHOLE.` · `IGNATIUS, ON THE ROAD TO ROME.` · `ONE, HOLY, CATHOLIC, APOSTOLIC.` · then, large: `EVERYWHERE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Picture the globe, slowly turning. Somewhere it's morning, and people are walking into a church. Somewhere it's midnight, and someone is praying alone by a candle. Somewhere a baby is being baptized, and somewhere a funeral is ending. Let the picture be as big as it wants to be. You're one person on it, breathing. If you pray, you can pray for all of them at once.
The Church. The ekklesia, the people called out, and catholic, meaning according to the whole: universal. Nineteenth word.
Your line: everywhere at once. Lagos, Manila, Texas, and wherever you're sitting. Day nineteen, done.

20.title: the saint who wrote about prayer like a friendship
20.hook: the saint who wrote about prayer like a friendship
20.carry: talk to him like a friend
20.howItsDone: Catholics keep a feast day for Saint Teresa of Ávila each year; her books on prayer, especially her Life and The Interior Castle, are still read, and Carmelite nuns and friars follow the reform she began.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Church, the ones called out, and catholic, meaning universal. Your line was everywhere at once. Today, one woman in one walled Spanish city. Day twenty.

Sit down to pray, or just to be quiet, and within a minute the mind has gone to lunch, or an argument from last week, or whether the car is locked. A woman in Spain, long ago, admitted in writing that for years prayer went like that for her. She would listen for the clock to strike, wishing the hour were over. She was a nun, and prayer was her whole job. Later the Church would call her a teacher of prayer for everyone.
screen: `SIT DOWN TO PRAY.` → `WITHIN A MINUTE: LUNCH.` → `SHE LISTENED FOR THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: Her name was Teresa, from the walled city of Ávila in Spain. She grew up in a big, lively family, and as a girl, by her own account, she cared more for books of knights and adventure, and for nice clothes, than for holiness. As a young woman she entered a Carmelite convent. And for years, she says in her autobiography, prayer was a struggle. Distracted, dry, going through the motions. Then, after a long time, something changed, and the way she described prayer afterward is the reason she's still read. Prayer, as she understands it, is nothing else than friendship: spending time often, alone, with the one we know loves us. Not a performance. Not a speech. Time with a friend. She wrote the way she talked: funny, blunt, full of kitchen pictures. She said God walks among the pots and pans. In another book, she pictures the soul as a castle made of a single diamond, with many rooms, and God living in the center. Prayer is the door you go in by. She also got a lot done. She founded new convents across Spain, traveling on bad roads in rough carts, arguing with bishops, and working with a young friar we know as John of the Cross. There's a story people love to tell: that after a cart tipped her into a muddy river, she complained to God, if this is how you treat your friends, no wonder you have so few. Nobody knows whether she really said it. But it sounds exactly like someone who talked to God like a friend. Long after her death, the Church named her a Doctor of the Church: a teacher for everyone.
screen: `ÁVILA. BOOKS OF KNIGHTS.` · `YEARS OF DRY PRAYER.` · `PRAYER IS FRIENDSHIP.` · `A CASTLE WITH MANY ROOMS.` · then, large: `TALK TO HIM LIKE A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, with no speech to give. Imagine a friend sitting across from you, one who knows you well and likes you anyway. Tell them, silently, one plain thing about your day. Not the polished version. Then just sit together without talking. When your mind wanders, and it will, come back the way you'd turn back to a friend after a distraction. If you pray, you can make that friend God.
Teresa of Ávila. The Carmelite nun who struggled with prayer for years, then described it as friendship with the one who loves us. Twentieth word.

21.title: the mountain ahead
21.hook: the mountain ahead; the prayers Jesus himself prayed
21.howItsDone: At every Mass a psalm is sung or said between the readings, and priests, religious and many lay Catholics pray the psalms through the day in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Teresa of Ávila, and prayer as friendship. Your line was talk to him like a friend. Today is the last day of camp one. Day twenty-one.
screen: `TALK TO HIM LIKE A FRIEND.` → `THE LAST DAY OF CAMP ONE.`

segments.voice: Look back down the hill for a second. Three weeks ago you started with the sign of the cross. Then the Eucharist. Confession. The rosary. The saints. Lent. Sacramentals. Grace. Mary. The Hail Mary. The Our Father. The Gospel. The sign of peace. Sunday. Candles. Easter. Francis. Mercy. The Church. Teresa. Twenty words: the words a Catholic hears every week. Now look up. There's a mountain ahead, and it's made of stories. But first, one more word, and it's the prayer book Jesus himself grew up praying.
screen: `TWENTY WORDS, DOWN THE HILL.` → `THE WORDS OF EVERY WEEK.` → `A MOUNTAIN MADE OF STORIES.`

segments.voice: The Psalms are a book of one hundred and fifty songs and prayers in the middle of the Bible. The Hebrew name is Tehillim: praises. Our word psalm comes from Greek, a song sung to a plucked string. They were Israel's prayer book and hymnal, and Jesus, a Jewish boy in Nazareth, likely grew up hearing them. Here's what surprises people: they aren't all nice. Some are joyful. Some are furious. Some are people in the dark asking God where he's gone. On the cross, in Matthew's Gospel, Jesus cries out the first line of one of those, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" That's a psalm. In that hour, he prays in words that were already old. And in another Gospel, his last words are from a psalm too: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." One detail, if you ever look them up in an older Catholic Bible: the numbers are often off by one. The Douay-Rheims follows the ancient Greek and Latin count, so the psalm Jesus cried on the cross is Psalm 21 there, and Psalm 22 in Bibles that follow the Hebrew. Same words, different count. The Church still prays them every day. At every Mass there's a psalm between the readings, the one from day twelve, sung back and forth. Priests, monks and nuns pray the psalms through the day in what's called the Liturgy of the Hours. And the rosary from day four, the poor man's psalter, grew up in their shadow. One hundred and fifty psalms, one for nearly every feeling a person can have. One hundred and fifty doors.

segments.voice: Here's the practice for the end of camp one. Ask yourself what you're actually feeling today, honestly. Glad. Tired. Angry. Lost. Grateful. Whatever it is, the Psalms have a door for it, and you don't have to clean it up first. Name the feeling in one word. Then breathe with it, not against it. If you pray, you can hand God that one word, just as it is.
The Psalms. One hundred and fifty praises, laments and songs, the prayer book Jesus himself prayed. Twenty-first word, and the last of camp one.
